Empirical Research Plan  
“Air Pollution and Infant Mortality in the United States: Evidence from the Great Recession”

────────────────────────────────────────
1. Identification Strategy
────────────────────────────────────────
Primary strategy Difference-in-Differences (DID) with an event-study extension and an Instrumental-Variables (IV) first stage.  
• DID: exploits the discrete break created by the Great Recession (≈ December 2007–June 2009). Counties that experienced larger pollution declines after the recession are “treated”; counties with small or no declines act as comparisons.  
• Event study: estimates dynamic effects and visually tests the parallel-trends assumption.  
• IV add-on (two-stage DID): recession-induced changes in local labor demand—proxied by the county’s pre-recession manufacturing share interacted with the national manufacturing shock—serve as instruments for pollution. This strengthens identification by purging remaining simultaneity between health outcomes and local pollution.

Why appropriate  
• Large, sudden, negative demand shock is plausibly exogenous to county-specific infant-health trends.  
• County- and year-level data allow rich fixed effects that absorb all time-invariant county factors and common national shocks.  
• IV handles potential remaining endogeneity of pollution (weather, local policy responses).

────────────────────────────────────────
2. Treatment and Control
────────────────────────────────────────
Treatment variable  
PM2.5_it = annual average concentration (µg/m³) for county i in year t.

Operational “treatment intensity”  
ΔPM2.5_i = (Mean PM2.5 2005-07) – (Mean PM2.5 2009-11).  
High-drop counties: ΔPM2.5_i above state-specific median → treated (binary DID)  
OR use ΔPM2.5_i continuously (preferred).

Control group  
Counties in the same state whose pollution dropped less than or equal to the median. State-specific definition minimizes policy heterogeneity and differential economic trends.

Treatment timing  
Post_t = 1 for 2009 onward (first full post-recession year), 0 for 2005-2007.  
(Optional placebo window 2002-2004).

Instrument (first stage)  
Recession Shock_i = Pre2007 share of employment in recession-sensitive industries (manufacturing + construction) × National % change in those sectors 2007-2009.  
Running variable & cutoff N/A (not RDD).

────────────────────────────────────────
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
────────────────────────────────────────
A1 Parallel trends: In the absence of the recession-induced pollution drop, infant mortality trends would have been similar across high- and low-drop counties.  
Plausibility: pre-trend testable; event-study coefficients for 2002-07 should be flat.

A2 No differential shocks: Other recession-related factors (e.g., income loss, Medicaid take-up) affect infant mortality similarly across counties once state-year fixed effects and observed economic controls are included.  
Plausibility: partly addressed by adding county-specific unemployment and poverty rates and state-year FE.

A3 Stable population composition: Birth-sorting or migration across counties is limited or not correlated with ΔPM2.5 beyond controls.  
Plausibility: short horizon (3-4 years) lowers risk; test with mother-level residence stability from natality files.

A4 IV exclusion: Recession Shock_i affects infant mortality only through its impact on PM2.5, not via other county-level channels after conditioning on economic covariates and state-year FE.  
Plausibility: reasonable but requires robustness (add employment/unemployment controls, use leave-one-out industry shocks).

────────────────────────────────────────
4. Threats to Identification and Remedies
────────────────────────────────────────
Threat 1: Simultaneous recession-driven income shocks could raise infant mortality, biasing estimates upward (toward finding harm).  
Remedy Add county-year controls for personal income, unemployment rate, SNAP/WIC caseloads; use state-year FE; IV approach further purges pollution from correlated economic shocks.

Threat 2: Measurement error in pollution (monitor coverage varies).  
Remedy Assign county pollution from nearest monitor with inverse-distance weighting; restrict to counties with ≥ 75 % monitor coverage; instrumented‐DID reduces attenuation bias.

Threat 3: Selective migration or fertility responses (families avoid polluted areas).  
Remedy (1) Fixed-effects already net out level differences; (2) Test for changes in county-level live-birth counts or maternal characteristics pre/post; (3) Run robustness restricting to mothers who resided in the county ≥ 1 year (from natality microdata).

────────────────────────────────────────
5. R Code Outline
────────────────────────────────────────
```r
# --- Packages ----
library(data.table)
library(fixest)        # fast fixed effects
library(ivreg)         # alternative IV
library(did)           # event study (Callaway–Sant’Anna)

# --- 1. Load Data ----
mort <- fread("county_infant_mortality.csv")   # county-year infant deaths & births
poll <- fread("county_pm25.csv")               # county-year PM2.5
econ <- fread("county_economic.csv")           # unemployment, income
ind  <- fread("county_industryshare.csv")      # 2006 employment shares

# --- 2. Merge & Construct Variables ----
dt <- Reduce(function(x,y) merge(x,y, by = c("fips","year"), all=TRUE),
             list(mort, poll, econ))

# Infant mortality per 1,000 live births
dt[, imr := 1000 * infant_deaths / live_births]

# Recession post indicator
dt[, post := as.integer(year >= 2009)]

# High-drop treatment indicator
pre_mean  <- dt[year %between% c(2005,2007), .(pm_pre = mean(pm25, na.rm=TRUE)), by=fips]
post_mean <- dt[year %between% c(2009,2011), .(pm_post = mean(pm25, na.rm=TRUE)), by=fips]
drops     <- merge(pre_mean, post_mean, by="fips")
drops[, dpm := pm_pre - pm_post]                           # positive = pollution fell
state_meds <- drops[, .(med = median(dpm, na.rm=TRUE)), by=state]
drops <- merge(drops, state_meds, by="state")
drops[, treat := as.integer(dpm > med)]
dt <- merge(dt, drops[, .(fips, dpm, treat)], by="fips")

# IV: recession shock (pre-industry share × national change)
nat_manu_change <- -0.12   # example: –12 % manufacturing jobs 2007-09
ind[, shock := manu_share2006 * nat_manu_change]
dt <- merge(dt, ind[, .(fips, shock)], by="fips")

# --- 3. Baseline DID (continuous treatment) ----
did1 <- feols(imr ~ post*dpm + unemployment + income_pc | fips + year,
              data = dt, cluster = ~state)
summary(did1)

# --- 4. Event-study (Callaway–Sant’Anna) ----
dt[, g := ifelse(treat==1, 2009, 0)]   # 0 = never-treated
att_gt <- att_gt(yname="imr", tname="year", idname="fips",
                 gname="g", xformla = ~ unemployment + income_pc,
                 data=dt, clustervars="state")
es_res <- aggte(att_gt, type="dynamic")
summary(es_res)
ggdid(es_res)

# --- 5. IV-DID ----
iv1 <- feols(imr ~ post*pm25 | fips + year |
             (post*pm25 ~ post*shock), data=dt, cluster=~state)
summary(iv1)

# --- 6. Robustness: county-specific linear trends ----
did2 <- feols(imr ~ post*dpm + unemployment + income_pc |
              fips + year + fips:year, data=dt, cluster=~state)
summary(did2)
```

────────────────────────────────────────
6. Expected Results
────────────────────────────────────────
Prior expectation: A 1 µg/m³ reduction in annual PM2.5 lowers infant mortality by roughly 0.5–1.0 deaths per 1,000 live births (consistent with epidemiological estimates). Direction: negative (cleaner air ⇒ fewer infant deaths).

────────────────────────────────────────
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID)
────────────────────────────────────────
C1 Pre-treatment trends parallel ……… 1  
C2 No interference/spillovers across counties ……… 0.5 (possible cross-county commuting)  
C3 No anticipatory effects ………… 1  
C4 No simultaneous shocks differentially correlated with treatment ……… 0.5  
C5 Stable measurement of outcome & treatment …… 1  

Total ≈ 4/5 → credible but needs robustness shown above.

────────────────────────────────────────
End of plan
